summary: Describes using AES in Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) mode, with an explicit initialization vector, in IPsec ESP to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, and connectionless integrity. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: One method that scrambles a message and also adds a tamper seal at the same time, instead of doing the two jobs separately.

questions: what is aes ccm in ipsec esp
how big is the aes ccm iv in esp
why must aes ccm use fresh keys
what are the ike transform ids for aes ccm
subtitle: How to use AES in CCM mode so one IPsec ESP pass both encrypts packets and checks that they were not tampered with.

tldr.problem: IPsec ESP needs confidentiality and integrity for each packet, and doing them as two separate steps costs extra work and packet overhead.
tldr.mechanism: AES CCM mode encrypts the payload with counter mode and computes an integrity check value in one operation. Each packet carries an 8-octet explicit IV, and the nonce is built from that IV plus a 3-octet salt.
tldr.outcome: ESP gets confidentiality, data origin authentication and connectionless integrity from one algorithm. The catch is that an IV must never repeat under the same key, so fresh keys are required.

today: RFC 4309 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself builds on RFC 4303 for ESP and RFC 3610 for CCM.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is a block cipher that can be used in many modes. RFC 4309 describes AES CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC) mode, with an explicit initialization vector (IV), as an IPsec ESP mechanism. It provides confidentiality, data origin authentication and connectionless integrity.

The document does not give an overview of IPsec. It points readers to RFC 4301 and RFC 2411 for how the pieces of IPsec fit together. CCM itself is defined in RFC 3610.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains how to use one combined lock-and-seal method inside IPsec's packet wrapper. The method scrambles the packet and also proves nobody changed it.

sections.title: CCM Parameters and Inputs
sections.content:
CCM has two parameters. M is the size of the integrity check value (ICV). CCM defines several sizes, but only multiples of four that are at least eight are permitted here. Implementations MUST support 8 and 16 octets and MAY support 12 octets. L is the size of the length field, and this specification supports only L = 4, which accommodates a full IPv6 Jumbogram.

Originator processing takes four inputs. The key is used both for the CBC-MAC and for counter mode encryption. AES key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits exist; 128 bits is the default and MUST be supported, while the others are optional. The nonce is 15 minus L octets, so implementations MUST support 11 octets. The payload includes the ESP Padding, Pad Length and Next Header fields. The AAD (additional authenticated data) covers data that is authenticated but not encrypted.
sections.plainLanguage: There are a few dials to set, like how long the tamper seal is and how big the secret key is. The document picks a small set of safe settings so everyone's devices can agree.

sections.title: The ESP Payload Layout
sections.content:
The ESP payload is the IV followed by the ciphertext, with the authentication data after that. The IV field MUST be eight octets. The encryptor chooses it so the same IV is used only once for a given key. Counting up for each packet and linear feedback shift registers (LFSRs) are given as common approaches. Because the IV travels in every packet, the receiver can still decrypt when datagrams are lost or reordered.

CCM needs no plaintext padding, but ESP still requires padding to 32-bit word-align the authentication data. The Padding, Pad Length and Next Header fields are concatenated with the plaintext before encryption. The ICV produced by CCM is carried in the Authentication Data field without further encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries its own little note saying which secret number was used, so the receiver can unlock it even if other packets get lost or arrive in the wrong order.

sections.title: Nonce and AAD Construction
sections.content:
The AES counter block is 16 octets: one octet for the CCM Flags, 4 octets for the block counter (set by L) and the remaining octets for the nonce. The nonce is built from a 24-bit salt and the 64-bit IV. The salt holds an unpredictable value assigned at the start of the security association. It need not be secret, but it MUST NOT be predictable beforehand.

This construction permits up to 2^32 blocks (68,719,476,736 octets) per packet, more key stream than any IPv6 Jumbogram needs.

The AAD carries the Security Parameters Index (SPI) and the sequence number. These fields are authenticated without being encrypted. There are two formats: one with a 32-bit sequence number and one with a 64-bit extended sequence number, sent in canonical network byte order with the high-order 32 bits first.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret number for each packet is made from a number chosen at the start of the conversation plus a fresh number per packet. The envelope's address labels are sealed in too, so nobody can swap them unnoticed.

sections.title: Packet Expansion and IKE Conventions
sections.content:
The only sources of packet growth are the IV and the ICV. The IV always adds 8 octets to the front of the payload, and the ICV size is set by M.

For key setup, IKE derives keying material (KEYMAT) that must be three octets longer than the AES key, with the extra three octets used as the salt. A 128-bit key therefore needs 19 octets, a 192-bit key needs 27 and a 256-bit key needs 35. This document does not define IKE Phase 1 use. For Phase 2, IANA assigned ESP transform identifiers 14 (8-octet ICV), 15 (12-octet ICV) and 16 (16-octet ICV). The Key Length attribute MUST be given as 128, 192 or 256.
sections.plainLanguage: The only extra baggage on each packet is the little note and the tamper seal. When two computers set up their secret key, they ask for three extra bytes to use as the starting number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CCM uses counter mode for confidentiality. If a counter value is used for more than one packet under the same key, the same key stream encrypts both. XORing the two ciphertexts then yields the XOR of the two plaintexts, which is relatively straightforward to separate. The RFC calls this a catastrophic failure of confidentiality.

For that reason AES CCM should not be used with statically configured keys, and implementations MUST use fresh keys, for example from IKE. IKE sets up separate keys for the two directions. If a mechanism establishes only a single key, the peers MUST assign different salt values to the SA to avoid counter block collisions.

With a 128-bit key, AES is vulnerable to the birthday attack after 2^64 blocks. Implementations SHOULD generate a fresh key before 2^64 blocks are encrypted, or use longer keys.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ever use the same secret number on two different messages, a snoop can compare them and learn what they say. So you must never reuse it, and you should always start from a freshly made key.

sections.title: Why an Explicit IV
sections.content:
The authors considered using the ESP sequence number instead of an explicit IV. They chose an explicit IV, noting that either approach prevents counter block collisions. The reasons given include that only the encryptor can ensure uniqueness, that adders, LFSRs and other techniques are all allowed, and that the decryptor is no more complex either way. Some implementations assign the sequence number outside the assurance boundary, and decoupling the IV from it accommodates them.

The 64-bit IV is also cheaper than CBC mode, which normally needs a full block for the IV and on average half a block of padding. The RFC says CCM with an explicit IV has about one-third of the overhead of AES CBC, constant for each packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors gave each packet its own number tag rather than borrowing another counter. That keeps things flexible and uses less extra space than the older way of doing it.
